about: One row per study of the numbered table on benchmarks/README.md. Every number carries the file and field it was read from. Built from the repository as it stood at commit 6ff1c2b, before the front pages were rewritten on 20 November 2026. Scores are errors: lower is better. "diff" is candidate minus reference. Independently checked against the result files and corrected on 20 November 2026. Row 26 (benchmarks/daily-sports-arm, published the same day in commits 318fa06 and 73c32c9, with benchmarks/daily-sports-arm/architecture from commits 13657c1 and badbd0b) was added afterwards, each of its files pinned to the checksum the study published; its numbers are names, not positions: rows are listed by what is forecast, so 26 comes before the two paper-only rows 24 and 25. Row 27 (benchmarks/daily-sports-limbs, commits 8e2b791, 7e6b4ed and b69df06) is the general learner's first published fit to real recordings. It carries "not_a_test": true: every score in it is on the people the model was fitted on, and it is in no count of tests (counts.general_learner_first_fit holds its own tallies). Row 28 (benchmarks/paired-wrist-forecast, commit 117ffa0) holds the general learner's three wrist fits with forearm EMG and scalp EEG, scored on the three people of rows 1 to 3; row 29 (benchmarks/wrist-forearm-correction, commit 7841010) carries "not_a_test": true, because its six people are the ones the earlier wrist models were fitted on. Both are listed after row 3; counts.general_learner holds the tallies of all five general-learner fits. "General learner" is the earlier name of what the front pages call the general model. "readme_claims_checked" compares each number that README.md printed at commit 6ff1c2b with its result file.

range.kind: change when any one of the three people is left out

primary.better_text: not published (the change stays positive whichever person is left out)

rule.text: No pass threshold. The plan (`protocol.json` → `outcomes`) fixes the main contrast in advance, the learner with EMG minus the learner on wrist history alone, and says: "No threshold, significance, population, new-cohort confirmation or live interpretation."
rule.met: no rule stated; primary contrast went against EMG

studies.happened: The general learner's first fits on a recording that also has muscle and brain signals: three fits, scored on three people already scored by rows 1 to 3. Forearm EMG made its wrist forecast worse, 5.432° → 5.866°, whichever person is left out. Scalp EEG on top took it to 5.822°, and the same fit fed another trial's EEG scored 5.826°. Row 1's learned forecast on wrist history alone, re-scored on the same trials, stayed lowest: 4.053°.
others: Wrong-trial controls: fed EMG from the next trial, the EMG fit scored 5.867° against 5.866° with its own (a difference of 0.0009°); fed EEG from the next trial, the EEG fit scored 5.826° against 5.822° (a difference of 0.0046°). The same swaps raised row 2's linear fits by 0.766° (EMG) and 0.252° (EEG). The linear fits depended on which trial the electrical signals came from; the general learner hardly did.
EEG after EMG: -0.045°, between -0.059° and -0.032° whichever person is left out; the fit fed another trial's EEG kept 0.040° of that 0.045°.
By axis, EMG's change was +0.626° for bending (extension) and +0.131° for sideways tilt (radial deviation).
The learner beat the linear fit on the same inputs in all three pairs (by 1.098°, 0.308° and 0.305°) and lost to row 1's learned forecast by 1.379° on the same inputs.

Row 2's linear fits and row 1's learned forecast are those rows' saved fits, re-scored here on 959 of their 960 trials; they are not new fits and enter no count. Row 2 had published 6.530°, 6.174°, 6.127° and 6.941°; row 1 had published 4.053° for the learned forecast and 7.925° for carry-forward.
The model's own 95% band held 92.2% and 92.6% (wrist history); 90.6% and 92.7% (with EMG); 89.3% and 93.5% (with EMG and EEG) of the readings (bending, sideways tilt).

Fit: three fresh fits of the shared learner, one per set of inputs, same seed, starting values and row order, four passes through the six fitting people's data; no tuning and no choice made on test scores (`protocol.json` → `fit`). The folder publishes the three fits and a command that runs them on an invented example (`predict.py`, `example.json`); `interfaces/paired-wrist-browser/` runs the same fits in a web browser. Neither is a result.

primary.question: With each person scored by models fitted on the other five, does a correction that also reads forearm EMG beat the same correction from wrist motion alone?

range.kind: change when any one of the six people is left out

rule.text: Set before fitting (`protocol.md`, "Outcomes, qualification and decision"): "A candidate forearm benefit requires the direction of the primary contrast and the comparison with the raw base to favor the aligned correction." On the pooled score both did (-0.116° and -0.069°); against the uncorrected forecast only 3 of 6 people did better. Applied to people already used for fitting, so it is not a test passed.
rule.met: on the fitting people only: both directions favoured the EMG correction on the pooled score; not a test

studies.happened: Not a test: the six people are the ones the earlier wrist models were fitted on. Each was scored by models fitted on the other five. A correction that also read forearm EMG beat the motion-only correction, 3.665° → 3.549°, for all six people, but beat the uncorrected forecast (3.618°) for only 3 of them. EMG helped at 0.75 s and 1 s after the cue and made the forecast worse at the four later moments.
others: At 0.75 s after the cue the motion-only correction missed by 7.441° and the EMG correction by 6.949°; at 1 s, 3.658° and 3.568°. From 1.25 s to 2 s the EMG correction was higher at every moment (2.541° against 2.423°, 1.940° against 1.837°, 1.652° against 1.313°, 1.267° against 0.941°).
The motion-only correction made the uncorrected forecast worse (+0.047°, 2 of 6 people better).

Controls: fed another person's EMG, the EMG correction scored 3.828°; fed its own EMG in reverse order, 3.720°; its own EMG beat both for all six people. The folder notes that movement and the contact of the electrodes can both change the EMG reading, and that neither control separates the two.
One network fitted on motion and EMG together scored 3.575° (2 of 6 people better than the uncorrected forecast); fed another person's EMG, 4.987°; fed its own EMG reversed, 4.462°.
By axis, the EMG correction's change against the motion-only correction was -0.180° for bending and -0.014° for sideways tilt.
The plan's check that the uncorrected forecast is a competent one: it beat carry-forward by 3.597° and the carried-forward velocity by 3.548°, for all six people.

The folder's own heading, "Forearm signals helped predict the early turn of a wrist", is true of the comparison it names; it is a result on people already used for fitting, not on new people, and the folder says so.

studies.happened: The general learner's first published fit to real recordings, and not a test: every score is on the four people it was fitted on. One checkpoint (45997 parameters) forecasts five accelerometers on a walker. On those four people it was lower than carry-forward at all five placements and lower than a linear fit made for each placement at four (not the torso). The rule set before training asks for more, lower than every available comparator for every person, and that was met at one placement, the left leg. Motion sensors only: no brain or muscle signal.
others: Rule, placement by placement (people of 4 for whom the general learner was lower than every available comparator): torso 1, right arm 0, left arm 3, right leg 3, left leg 4. Against the linear fit alone: torso 1, right arm 4, left arm 3, right leg 3, left leg 4. Against carry-forward: 4 of 4 at every placement.
Torso: the linear fit had the lower pooled score (0.696 against 0.722), and the general learner was lower for 1 person of 4.

Right arm: the general learner (0.806) was lower than the linear fit (0.869) for all four people, and higher than row 26's transformer (0.668) for all four. That transformer was fitted for the right arm alone, on these same four people, so both scores are on fitting data.
Left arm and right leg: lower pooled score than both comparators (0.727 against 0.770; 1.891 against 1.967), but one person at each lost to the linear fit, so the rule failed.
Left leg: 1.837 against 1.929 for the linear fit and 3.168 for carry-forward, lower for all four people: the one placement where the rule was met.
Fit: 12 epochs, 3180 optimiser updates, one process on a CPU. Reopening the checkpoint reproduced every stored prediction (largest difference 0).

The result file also holds, for each placement, how many of the fitting people's readings fell inside the model's own 95% band: between 92.9% and 97.6% across the fifteen axes. On fitting data that says little; the folder README says the band is untested on a new walker.

The folder holds launchers and a page (`viewer.html`, served by `serve.py` on the reader's own computer) that runs the checkpoint on a recorded window or a pasted one, and a capability table (`CAPABILITIES.md`) that sets this sensor forecast beside the controls of the game and a camera preview; neither is a result.

A fit of the same learner to the right arm alone, run on row 26's two test people, is published in `benchmarks/daily-sports-arm/architecture/earlier-results.json`; its people and its target are row 26's, so it is reported there.
